title: Khandayat: land, service and community history
lead: How did a name associated with the sword become a community identity? Khandayat history leads through forts and fields, inherited duties, changing social boundaries and the traditions kept within households.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

sections.title: A name is a starting point

paragraphs.text: In 1896, Jogendra Nath Bhattacharya explained Khandait as “swordsman”. His account connected the name with military work and described people turning increasingly to agriculture. It is a dated description of how the community was understood, not a founding charter. The meaning of a name cannot by itself tell us when every family acquired it.

The sources examined here do not establish one ruler creating the whole community on one date. They help answer a different question: through what institutions, livelihoods and claims did Khandayat identity take shape?

Akio Tanabe places early-modern Khurda within a landscape of forts, forest clearings and cultivated land. Villages and fields grew around forts. Forest inhabitants became warriors, cultivators and herdsmen alongside newcomers from the plains. Defence depended on a working countryside.
Khurda’s kingdom dates, about 1570–1804, are not a caste’s lifespan. Tanabe explains connections between service, settlement and livelihoods, not the ancestry of every Khandayat family across Odisha.

In his study of the Paika rebellion, Tanabe shows how military and administrative positions, carrying land or payment, could become hereditary. Such arrangements help explain how work and family identity became linked. They do not make Paika and Khandayat interchangeable: a service establishment could recruit people from different communities.

His census comparison is especially revealing. In Puri district, the recorded Khandayat population rose from 8,193 in 1891 to 112,571 in 1931; the Chasa count fell from 273,715 to 231,021. Tanabe interprets this through changing identification and claims to status. These figures concern historical census categories in one district. They cannot be read simply as natural population growth, or used to declare every Chasa a Khandayat.

Bhattacharya distinguished Mahanayaka or Sreshta Khandaits from Paik or Chasa Khandaits, and listed titles including Jena, Nayaka, Rout, Samanta and Senapati. This preserves a nineteenth-century classification, with the author’s assumptions about social rank. It is not a complete map of present communities. A surname alone cannot verify an ancestor’s office.

Origin traditions answer another kind of question. Tanabe records a Saori Khandayat account that connects royal descent with Saora ancestry. Read as a narrated claim to belonging, it belongs in the history of community memory. It does not prove a shared genealogy or turn a tribal identity into a caste synonym.
paragraphs.locator: pp35–36; narrated tradition, no literal descent verification

paragraphs.text: Military titles tell only part of this history. Yumiko Tokita-Tanabe’s fieldwork among Khandayat women in Garh Manitri, Khurda, ran from April 1991 to November 1992. Her study describes women preparing household and ancestral offerings, including food and water. Domestic work and ritual knowledge also sustained belonging; this evidence comes from a particular village and period.

The same study records turmeric and oil used in a first-menstruation bathing ritual. Turmeric use therefore has a documented local setting. This does not establish the history of today’s staged wedding “Haldi” ceremony: the occasion, form and transmission of a custom matter as much as its ingredients. One village account cannot decide what all Odia families traditionally practised.

For a family history, start with the village, the names people use for themselves, older documents and the accounts of different generations. Ask which duties and customs people remember, who taught them, and what changed. Regional histories can then be connected without forcing them into a single origin story.
